name: Numbers on Tree
description: Evlampiy was gifted a rooted tree. The vertices of the tree are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Each of its vertices also has an integer $$$a_i$$$ written on it. For each vertex $$$i$$$, Evlampiy calculated $$$c_i$$$ — the number of vertices $$$j$$$ in the subtree of vertex $$$i$$$, such that $$$a_j \lt a_i$$$. Illustration for the second example, the first integer is $$$a_i$$$ and the integer in parentheses is $$$c_i$$$ After the new year, Evlampiy could not remember what his gift was! He remembers the tree and the values of $$$c_i$$$, but he completely forgot which integers $$$a_i$$$ were written on the vertices. Help him to restore initial integers!
input_specification: The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ $$$(1 \leq n \leq 2000)$$$ — the number of vertices in the tree. The next $$$n$$$ lines contain descriptions of vertices: the $$$i$$$-th line contains two integers $$$p_i$$$ and $$$c_i$$$ ($$$0 \leq p_i \leq n$$$; $$$0 \leq c_i \leq n-1$$$), where $$$p_i$$$ is the parent of vertex $$$i$$$ or $$$0$$$ if vertex $$$i$$$ is root, and $$$c_i$$$ is the number of vertices $$$j$$$ in the subtree of vertex $$$i$$$, such that $$$a_j \lt a_i$$$. It is guaranteed that the values of $$$p_i$$$ describe a rooted tree with $$$n$$$ vertices.
output_specification: If a solution exists, in the first line print " YES ", and in the second line output $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_i$$$ $$$(1 \leq a_i \leq {10}^{9})$$$. If there are several solutions, output any of them. One can prove that if there is a solution, then there is also a solution in which all $$$a_i$$$ are between $$$1$$$ and $$$10^9$$$. If there are no solutions, print " NO ".
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1286B — Numbers on Tree [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
